newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan stocks seen trapped into further tailspin.
newsitem.headline: Japan stocks seen trapped into further tailspin.

text.p: Japanese stocks could be trapped in a tailspin amid unmitigated gloom over the economy and the lack of any clear support level that would spark investor buying.

Some analysts said the key 225-share Nikkei stock index could plummet towards the low of 14,295 marked in July 1995, the second major bottom on charts after the bursting of the "bubble economy" of inflated Japanese assets in the early 1990s.
They said the government has been trapped in a dead end in hammering out any effective steps to spur confidence in the economy and rescue stock prices.

On Friday, the market's Nikkei average plunged another 4.26 percent to 17,303.65, continuing the downward spiral without any firm support points standing in the way from around 21,800 in early December.
"We can't see any reasonable supporting points," said Koichi Ichiko, general manager of the securities investment department at Asahi Mutual Life Insurance Co.
"It all depends on whether the government will propose any new policies."
But some market watchers said the government had nothing to offer the market to cheer it up.
Tamizo Kimura, chief strategist at Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities & Economics, said that in the worst scenario, the key Nikkei average may dive to the mid-14,000 level.
"The debacle this time is caused by negative factors that didn't exist in the last two dives. There are no available measures left for the government," Kimura said.
Japan has no room to ease its monetary policy, as the key lending rate has already been locked at 0.5 percent since September 1995.
On the fiscal front, there is little chance of Japan being able to spend its way out of its economic slump.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has made tackling the mounting budget deficits, already among the highest in the industrialised world, the top priority.
"There is no immediate remedy," admitted top government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama.
He added that prices should go back up if Japan continued to strengthen its economic fundamentals through various reforms.

The pessimistic outlook accelerated late last month when the government endorsed a planned rise in the sales tax to five percent in April from the current three percent and end special income tax cuts.
Growing worries over the health of financial firms added to the downtrend.
Shinichi Ichikawa, strategist at Credit Lyonnais Securities, said he expected the Nikkei 225 to start bouncing back after dipping briefly below 17,000.
"The stock market will have to go through hard times until the middle of February," he said. "But if the Nikkei 225 breaches 17,000, buying demand is expected to slow the fall."
